learning_outcomes.text: Ability to understand the magnitudes that define the different properties characterizing the behavior of industrial materials.
Ability to control the properties of materials based on their atomic structures and defects.
Ability to fluently handle binary equilibrium diagrams and the fundamentals of ternary diagrams.
Ability to design heat treatments in order to modify the microstructure and properties of steels, cast irons, and non-ferrous alloys.
Knowledge of industrial ceramics and understanding of the relationship between their structures, manufacturing processes, properties, and uses.
Knowledge of industrial plastics and understanding of the relationship between their structures, properties, and uses.
Ability to use diverse materials and combine them appropriately to design composite materials with controlled properties.
Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing versatility to adapt to new situations.
Knowledge of atomic structures and their defects and ability to control material properties by modifying atomic structures with defects.
Knowledge of the magnitudes that define properties characterizing the behavior of industrial materials.
Knowledge of phase diagrams enabling them to fluently handle binary equilibrium diagrams and the fundamentals of ternary diagrams.
Knowledge of the fundamentals of material science, technology, and chemistry. Understanding the relationship between microstructure, synthesis or processing, and the properties of metallic materials.
Knowledge to design heat treatments in order to modify the microstructure and properties of steels, cast irons, and non-ferrous alloys.
Knowledge to use diverse materials and combine them appropriately to design composite materials with controlled properties.
Knowledge to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning.
Knowledge for performing measurements, calculations, evaluations, appraisals, expert reports, studies, reports, work plans, and other similar tasks.
Basic knowledge of concepts related to product verification and inspection and ability to handle specifications, regulations, and mandatory standards.
Identify the structures of fundamental crystalline solids and assess the importance of different structural defects.
Interpret the different properties of materials and also be able to determine them experimentally using appropriate testing techniques.
Interpret equilibrium diagrams and use them in material development.

Fluently handle the Fe-C diagram, transformation curves, evaluate the influence of alloying elements in these products, the practical use of Jominy hardenability curves of steels, and the effects of heat treatments.
Discern the main characteristics of non-ferrous alloys of industrial interest that justify their application, assess the importance of alloying elements, and the effects of heat treatments.
Differentiate between different families of plastic materials, ceramics, and composite materials, their main characteristics, advantages, and limitations for industrial use.
Ability to define the fundamental characteristics that describe crystalline structures.
Ability to use diffusion laws for various calculations.
Ability to determine the conventional mechanical properties of industrial materials by performing corresponding experimental tests.
Ability to determine electrical, magnetic, thermal, and optical properties using experimental methods.
Ability to interpret binary equilibrium diagrams and to plot points and determine the phases present in ternary diagrams.
Ability to interpret the Fe-C diagram and the transformation curves of steels and cast irons to modify their microstructure and properties through mechanical and thermal treatments.
Ability to prepare metallographic specimens, perform heat treatments, and interpret the microstructures of iron-based materials.
Ability to interpret the basic equilibrium diagrams of the most important non-ferrous metallic alloys and use them to define their characteristic heat treatments.
Ability to handle and interpret equilibrium diagrams in ceramic systems and to control their properties based on their manufacturing processes.
Ability to interpret the mechanical properties of plastics based on their structural characteristics and manufacturing processes.
Ability to calculate the properties of composite materials from those of their constituent simple materials.
To foster in the student a desire for the acquisition of scientific knowledge.
To lay the foundations for the student to be able to apply the acquired knowledge in engineering.
Formation of an open, critical, and entrepreneurial spirit.
Correctly handle the recommended physical symbology in the fields of Mechanics and Thermodynamics, both in terms of magnitudes and units.
Understand the physical-mathematical description of particle motion and know the magnitudes that quantify it.
Understand the laws and theorems that relate the motion of particles to the causes that provoke it.
Understand the concepts and principles necessary for the study of heat exchange processes in closed systems of ideal gases.
Learn and put into practice problem-solving strategies related to the fields of Mechanics and Thermodynamics.
Acquire skills related to laboratory work and to the treatment of measurements and errors in the fields of Mechanics and Thermodynamics.

syllabus_topics: Structures of solids, structural defects, and diffusion phenomena
Solidification and transformations in solid state. Equilibrium diagrams
Ferrous alloys: steels and cast irons. Iron-carbon diagram and heat treatments
Non-Metallic Materials: ceramics, polymers, and composite materials
Mechanical, electrical, magnetic, thermal, and optical properties of materials
Microstructural observation of steels and cast irons. Grain size (P6)
Tensile and compression testing in different materials (P11)
Electronic configuration and types of bonds (Topic 2)
Material structure. Crystalline systems. Crystalline defects (Topic 3)
Mechanical properties I: tensile, hardness, and toughness. Introduction to fracture mechanics (Topic 12)
Mechanical properties II: fatigue and creep (Topic 13)

assessment_methods.method: Final exam (traditional evaluation) laboratory practices section
Final exam (extraordinary evaluation) laboratory practices section
Final exam (differentiated evaluation) laboratory practices section

assessment_rules: For continuous evaluation, the final exam score (up to 7 points) is added to the partial exam score (up to 3 points). To pass, a minimum score of 4 out of 10 must be obtained in the final exam, with at least one-third of the value achieved in each of its three parts (theory, problems, laboratory practices). The course is passed with 5 points or more. For traditional, extraordinary, and differentiated evaluations, the passing criteria is the same for the final exam (minimum 4/10 with one-third from each part) and the overall pass mark (5 points or more). The submission of proposed exercises and completed lab reports is mandatory for continuous evaluation but does not directly affect the grade.
